newsitem.title: USA: TIN - U.S. traders more bearish for 1997 prices.
newsitem.headline: TIN - U.S. traders more bearish for 1997 prices.

text.p: Tin prices in the first half of 1997 are set to remain at current levels or barely move above this year's highs at best, U.S. tin traders forecast.
Seven members of the American Tin Trade Association gave their forecasts ahead of this week's meeting in New York.
Robert Goldsobel of RMT Metals said prices were heading lower because of production increases in Peru, Indonesia and China.
"Demand will be fairly good in 1997, but I think the growth is mainly in chemicals and special applications, and not so much in tin-plate," Goldsobel said.

Lily Harlina of Indometal Corp also believed that more production in Peru and Brazil will limit price gains. "And finally, Chinese production, which has been pretty much restrained this year, will bounce back in 1997 with no ATPC quotas to worry about."

But Steve Napolitano of Toyota Tshusho America Inc thinks tin, like the rest of the base metals complex will be hostage to copper's fortunes once again in 1997. "We saw this year that in spite of improving fundamentals, tin prices were influenced more by the Sumitomo crisis," Napolitano said.
F&S International's Tim Reyes said he was less bearish than he was earlier this year, but prices could come under pressure if Peru, Brazil and China exceed production forecasts.
"Demand also has to start kicking in, especially in Europe and the Far East," Reyes added.
Jack Russell of Schilberg Metals expected a "flat and unexciting" market in the first half of 1997. But unknowns such as new U.S. government stockpile sales policies could upset the trend.
Amalgamet's Bernard Silverstein saw the downside as being limited, due to low stocks and a resumption of buying could send prices higher.
"I also don't see the Chinese being as big a factor as they were in the past," Silverstein said.
Finally, Paranapanema's Lueder Weseloh also believed prices next year will work higher due to low stocks.
If demand picked up or stayed the same, production was unlikely to increase.

"Instead a buying panic could easily set in, as the market realizes there is not much tin around," Weseloh said "Finally, Chinese exports will probably be low again next year, and increased Peruvian and Indonesian production has already been discounted."
LME cash tin settled at $5,820 per tonne Monday, near the year's lows.
